desc:
You start with a set of distinct integers stored in a binary search tree (possibly empty), and then receive a list of operations [type, x] to apply in order:

  • [0, x]: insert the value x into the set. It is not in the set yet.
  • [1, x]: delete the value x from the set. It is in the set.
  • [2, x]: query the x-th smallest value currently in the set (counting from 1). The set has at least x values.
  • [3, x]: query how many values currently in the set are strictly smaller than x.

Return the answers to the queries (types 2 and 3) in the order they were asked. Updates produce no output.

The tree only describes the starting set; you may use any structure you like afterwards. A solution that walks the whole set for every query is too slow: aim for about O(log n) per operation.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [5,2,7,-1,3,6] is the tree whose root 5 has left child 2 and right child 7; node 2 has no left child and right child 3; node 7 has left child 6 and no right child.

Example

tree = [5,2,8], ops = [[2,2],[0,6],[3,7],[1,2],[2,2],[3,100]]
Output: [5,3,6,3]
Start {2,5,8}: 2nd smallest is 5. Insert 6 gives {2,5,6,8}: values below 7 are 2, 5, 6 (3 of them). Delete 2 gives {5,6,8}: 2nd smallest is 6. Values below 100: 3.
constraints: 0 ≤ initial number of nodes ≤ 3,000; the tree is a valid BST with distinct values
1 ≤ ops.length ≤ 6,000; at least one op is a query
0 ≤ every value and every x in types 0, 1, 3 ≤ 1,000,000
Inserts never duplicate a value; deletes always remove an existing value; x in type 2 is within the current set size
hints: Keeping a sorted list and using binary search handles the queries, but each insert and delete shifts O(n) items. Can you make updates and order queries both logarithmic?
Order statistics need counts. Think about a structure that stores, for ranges of values, how many members are present. All values appearing in the input are known in advance.

Sort and deduplicate every value from the tree and from the inserts, and use a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) over that coordinate list with 1 for present and 0 for absent. rank = prefix sum; k-th smallest = binary descent on the Fenwick tree.
editorial: The classic answer is a balanced BST augmented with subtree sizes, which gives O(log n) insert, delete, rank and k-th. An easier route when all values can be read in advance is offline coordinate compression: collect the initial values and every inserted value, sort them, and map each to an index. Then a Fenwick tree over these indices stores 1 for a present value and 0 otherwise.

Insert and delete are point updates; rank(x) is a prefix sum over the indices of values smaller than x (use binary search to find the boundary index); the x-th smallest value is found by the Fenwick descent: starting from the highest power of two, step forward while the accumulated count stays below x. The next position is the answer's index. Total time O((n + q) log (n + q)), memory O(n + q).
